section.title: Isaac and Abimelech
section.sectionRationale: This is the only chapter given wholly to Isaac, and it shows the promise made to Abraham renewed to the son. Isaac repeats his father's faith and his father's failures, God blesses him amid famine and strife over wells, and a pagan king again seeks a treaty because God is plainly with him.
section.thesis: God renews the covenant promise to Isaac and blesses him abundantly, so that even his enemies confess the LORD is with him; the God of Abraham proves faithful to the next generation, carrying His promise on despite famine, fear, and conflict.
section.frameNote: Six scenes: the promise confirmed to Isaac; the sister-wife deception; prosperity and contested wells; the LORD's appearing at Beersheba; the covenant with Abimelech; Esau's grievous marriages.

units.label: The promise confirmed to Isaac
units.note: I will be with you and bless you

verses.text: Now there was another famine in the land, subsequent to the one that had occurred in Abraham’s time. And Isaac went to Abimelech king of the Philistines at Gerar.
The LORD appeared to Isaac and said, “Do not go down to Egypt. Settle in the land where I tell you.

Stay in this land as a foreigner, and I will be with you and {{barak|bless}} you. For I will give all these lands to you and your offspring, and I will confirm the oath that I swore to your father Abraham.
I will make your descendants as numerous as the stars in the sky, and I will give them all these lands, and through your offspring all nations of the earth will be blessed,
because Abraham listened to My voice and kept My charge, My commandments, My statutes, and My laws.”
So Isaac settled in Gerar.

But when the men of that place asked about his wife, he said, “She is my sister.” For he was afraid to say, “She is my wife,” since he thought to himself, “The men of this place will kill me on account of Rebekah, because she is so beautiful.”
When Isaac had been there a long time, Abimelech king of the Philistines looked down from the window and was surprised to see Isaac caressing his wife Rebekah.
Abimelech sent for Isaac and said, “So she is really your wife! How could you say, ‘She is my sister’?” Isaac replied, “Because I thought I might die on account of her.”
“What is this you have done to us?” asked Abimelech. “One of the people could easily have slept with your wife, and you would have brought guilt upon us.”
So Abimelech warned all the people, saying, “Whoever harms this man or his wife will surely be put to death.”
Now Isaac sowed seed in the land, and that very year he reaped a hundredfold. And the LORD blessed him,
and he became richer and richer, until he was exceedingly wealthy.
He owned so many flocks and herds and servants that the Philistines envied him.
So the Philistines took dirt and stopped up all the wells that his father’s servants had dug in the days of his father Abraham.
Then Abimelech said to Isaac, “Depart from us, for you are much too powerful for us.”
So Isaac left that place and encamped in the Valley of Gerar and settled there.

Isaac reopened the wells that had been dug in the days of his father Abraham, which the Philistines had stopped up after Abraham died. And he gave these wells the same names his father had given them.
Then Isaac’s servants dug in the valley and found a well of fresh water there.
But the herdsmen of Gerar quarreled with Isaac’s herdsmen and said, “The water is ours!” So he named the well Esek, because they contended with him.
Then they dug another well and quarreled over that one also; so he named it Sitnah.
He moved on from there and dug another well, and they did not quarrel over it. He named it {{rachab|Rehoboth}} and said, “At last the LORD has made room for us, and we will be fruitful in the land.”

units.label: The LORD appears at Beersheba
units.note: do not be afraid, for I am with you

verses.text: From there Isaac went up to Beersheba,

and that night the LORD appeared to him and said, “I am the God of your father Abraham. Do not be afraid, for I am with you. I will bless you and multiply your descendants for the sake of My servant Abraham.”
So Isaac built an altar there and called on the name of the LORD, and he pitched his tent there. His servants also dug a well there.

units.label: The covenant with Abimelech
units.note: the LORD has been with you

verses.text: Later, Abimelech came to Isaac from Gerar, with Ahuzzath his adviser and Phicol the commander of his army.
“Why have you come to me?” Isaac asked them. “You hated me and sent me away.”
“We can plainly see that the LORD has been with you,” they replied. “We recommend that there should now be an oath between us and you. Let us make a {{berith|covenant}} with you
that you will not harm us, just as we have not harmed you but have done only good to you, sending you on your way in peace. And now you are blessed by the LORD.”
So Isaac prepared a feast for them, and they ate and drank.
And they got up early the next morning and swore an oath to each other. Then Isaac sent them on their way, and they left him in peace.
On that same day, Isaac’s servants came and told him about the well they had dug. “We have found water!” they told him.
So he called it Shibah, and to this day the name of the city is Beersheba.

units.label: Esau's grievous marriages
units.note: a grief to Isaac and Rebekah

verses.text: When Esau was forty years old, he took as his wives Judith daughter of Beeri the Hittite and Basemath daughter of Elon the Hittite.
And they brought grief to Isaac and Rebekah.

barak.gloss: To bless, to bestow life giving favour and good, from a root linked to kneeling. God's blessing is His active goodness that makes fruitful and prospers. The word runs like a refrain through this chapter, as God blesses Isaac in famine, in harvest, and in the eyes of watching enemies.

rachab.gloss: To be wide, broad, or roomy, to make space. Isaac names a well Rehoboth, broad places, because at last the LORD has made room for him after repeated conflict. The word pictures God enlarging His people's place and giving room to be fruitful when the way has been cramped by strife.

berith.gloss: A binding agreement, treaty, or covenant, often sealed with an oath, a meal, or a sacrifice. Here it is a peace pact Abimelech seeks with Isaac because God is with him. The same word carries the far weightier covenant God Himself makes and confirms with the patriarchs, and finally the new covenant in Christ.

basic.context: This chapter follows Isaac through a famine, a lie about his wife, disputes over wells, and a treaty with Abimelech. Woven through it all, God renews to Isaac the very promises He made to Abraham. The key question is whether God's covenant will hold with the son, and the chapter answers with a resounding yes despite Isaac's flaws.
basic.hermeneutics: This is history that also teaches. Isaac clearly echoes Abraham, both his faith and his failures, and the writer wants us to see the promise passing intact to the next generation. The question is how God's faithfulness relates to the patriarchs' weakness, and the answer centres on grace, not merit.
basic.originalLanguages: The word barak, to bless, sounds again and again as God prospers Isaac. When strife over water finally eases, Isaac names a well Rehoboth, from rachab, to make room, praising God for room to be fruitful. Abimelech then seeks a berith, a covenant of peace, confessing that the LORD is with Isaac.
basic.typology: Isaac, the son who inherits his father's promise, foreshadows the greater Son who inherits all the promises of God. The blessing that flows to the nations through Isaac's offspring points to Christ, and the room God makes at Rehoboth pictures the wide welcome of God's grace.
basic.christ: The promise renewed to Isaac, that through his offspring all nations will be blessed, reaches its goal in Christ. Where Isaac lied out of fear, Christ spoke the truth even at the cost of His life, and He is the true Seed in whom the covenant is finally secured.
basic.god: God is faithful, present, and generous. He renews His oath to Isaac for Abraham's sake, blesses him in famine, and makes room for him amid conflict. He is the God who says do not be afraid, for I am with you, and He makes even enemies acknowledge His presence.
basic.crossReferences: Genesis 12 and 22 hold the promises God renews here. Genesis 20 and 21 record Abraham's parallel sister-wife episode and treaty. Romans 4 celebrates the promise to Abraham's offspring, fulfilled in Christ.
basic.oneStory: God carries His promise safely from Abraham to Isaac, blessing him so richly that even his enemies see the LORD is with him. The covenant advances by grace despite human weakness, moving on toward Christ, in whom all nations are blessed.

context.literary:
Genesis 26 interrupts the story of the twins. Chapter 25 ended with the birthright sold, chapter 27 begins with the blessing stolen, and in between the narrator sets a whole chapter about Isaac on his own. The twins are never mentioned until Esau's marriages in verses 34 and 35, and the sister-wife ruse would hardly be believable with two grown sons in the tent. Many readers therefore take the chapter to be arranged by theme rather than strict sequence. It pauses the family quarrel to show what Isaac has inherited.

The chapter is framed by two appearances of the LORD, verses 2 to 5 at Gerar and verse 24 at Beersheba. Between them the story alternates between trouble and blessing: famine, then promise; fear and deception, then protection; envy and expulsion, then a hundredfold harvest; quarrels over wells, then room. The word 'bless' sounds five times, in verses 3, 4, 12, 24 and 29, and the last time it is on the lips of a Philistine king.

The chapter is also built out of echoes. Almost every scene repeats something from Abraham's life: the famine of Genesis 12:10, the wife passed off as a sister in Genesis 12 and 20, the dispute over a well in Genesis 21:25, the treaty with Abimelech and Phicol and the naming of Beersheba in Genesis 21:22-31. Abraham is named again and again, 'in the days of his father Abraham,' verses 1, 15 and 18. Isaac even reopens his father's wells and gives them 'the same names his father had given them.' The repetitions are deliberate. Isaac's life is the story of a son walking in the tracks his father left, for better and for worse.

The sequence of wells gives the chapter its movement: Esek, contention; Sitnah, hostility; Rehoboth, room; and finally Shibah, oath, at Beersheba. The names trace a path from conflict to peace, and the chapter closes with the discord that will drive chapter 27, two Hittite wives who bring grief to Isaac and Rebekah.
context.historical:
Gerar lay in the western Negev, in the region Genesis 20:1 describes as 'between Kadesh and Shur.' It was the natural first stop for a herdsman heading toward Egypt in a famine, as Abraham had done in Genesis 12:10 and as Jacob's sons would do in Genesis 42:1-2. Egypt's river made it the breadbasket of the region when the rains failed in Canaan.

Abimelech may be a royal title or a dynastic name rather than a personal one. A king of that name dealt with Abraham decades earlier, Genesis 20 and 21, and the heading of Psalm 34 uses it for the Philistine king David met, who is called Achish in 1 Samuel 21:10. Phicol the army commander likewise appears in both generations.

Isaac does something unusual for a patriarch: he sows seed. The patriarchs were mainly pastoralists, but seasonal planting was possible in the Negev in a good year. A hundredfold return was extraordinary, and the narrator attributes it plainly to the LORD, verse 12.

In that dry country wells were wealth and life. To stop up a well was an act of war; much later Israel's armies were told to 'stop up every spring' in Moab, 2 Kings 3:19. The Philistines' filling of Abraham's wells was a way of erasing his claim to the land. Reopening them and restoring their names was a way of reasserting it.

Treaties in this world were sealed by oath and by a shared meal, as here in verses 30 and 31 and later between Jacob and Laban, Genesis 31:46 and 31:54. Beersheba itself later marked the southern edge of Israel in the phrase 'from Dan to Beersheba,' Judges 20:1, so the first hearers knew the town Isaac named 'to this day,' verse 33.
context.canonical:
This chapter is where the promise to Abraham becomes the promise to Abraham and Isaac. God says He will 'confirm the oath that I swore to your father Abraham,' verse 3, taking up the oath of Genesis 22:16-18 almost word for word, including 'through your offspring all nations of the earth will be blessed.' From here on Scripture speaks of the covenant with the three patriarchs together. God remembers 'His covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob,' Exodus 2:24, and Psalm 105:9 speaks of 'the oath He swore to Isaac.' God names Himself to Moses as 'the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob,' Exodus 3:6, and Jesus argues from that very title that God 'is not the God of the dead, but of the living,' Matthew 22:32.

The phrase 'for the sake of My servant Abraham,' verse 24, sets a pattern. Later God spares Judah 'for the sake of My servant David,' 1 Kings 11:13 and 2 Kings 19:34. Blessing flowing to others because of one servant's standing with God is a thread that runs to the gospel, where 'through the obedience of the one man the many will be made righteous,' Romans 5:19.

The command 'Do not go down to Egypt,' verse 2, stands in contrast with God's later word to Jacob, 'Do not be afraid to go down to Egypt,' Genesis 46:3, and with the prophets' warning, 'Woe to those who go down to Egypt for help,' Isaiah 31:1. The Philistine confession, 'We can plainly see that the LORD has been with you,' anticipates Zechariah 8:23, where the nations grasp a Jew's robe and say, 'Let us go with you, for we have heard that God is with you.' Hebrews 11:9 remembers Isaac among those who 'lived in tents' as heirs of the promise, and Paul says the promise made Abraham's offspring 'heir of the world,' Romans 4:13, which fits God's plural in verses 3 and 4, 'all these lands.'

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Israel needed to know that the promise did not die with Abraham. The chapter shows the covenant passing to the second generation intact: the same land, the same offspring, the same blessing for the nations, confirmed by the same oath. For a people in the wilderness, hearing of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob as their fathers, this was a pledge that God's word outlives the people who first receive it.

The author also meant Israel to learn from where Isaac went and did not go. In famine God told him to stay in the land rather than look to Egypt, and in the land God made him prosper. Israel would face the same temptation to seek security from Egypt, and the chapter says that God's presence in the land is better than Egypt's grain.

The chapter also teaches how the chosen should live among neighbours. Isaac yields well after well rather than fight, and God makes room for him. When his enemies come, he feeds them and sends them away in peace. The blessing on Israel was meant to be visible to the nations, so that outsiders would say, as Abimelech did, 'you are blessed by the LORD.' Finally, verse 5 frames Abraham's obedience in the vocabulary of the law, teaching Israel that the heirs of the promise are those who listen to God's voice.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Isaac's lie about Rebekah is recorded, not recommended. The narrator lets a pagan king deliver the rebuke, 'What is this you have done to us?', which echoes God's own question to Eve in Genesis 3:13. Isaac's fear is shown to be both groundless and dangerous: no one had threatened him, and his deception nearly brought guilt on others.

The hundredfold harvest and great wealth describe what God did for Isaac as the bearer of the promise. They are not a formula guaranteeing that every faithful believer will prosper materially; Hebrews 11 lists many faithful people who died destitute.

What does carry over is the direction of the story. God's word to 'stay in this land' called for trust in God's presence over visible security. Isaac's refusal to fight for each well, and his hospitality to former enemies, fit the later command, 'If it is possible on your part, live at peace with everyone,' Romans 12:18, and the promise of Proverbs 16:7 that when a man's ways please the LORD, He makes even his enemies live at peace with him.

debates.question: Why does the narrator record Isaac repeating Abraham's sister-wife deception?

views.label: To show the patriarchs' real weakness
views.case: Scripture tells the truth about its heroes. Isaac copies his father's fear as well as his faith, using almost the same excuse, 'I thought I might die on account of her,' compare Genesis 20:11. The promise evidently does not rest on the moral strength of those who carry it.

views.label: To magnify God's protecting faithfulness
views.case: By recording the failure and the rescue, the story shows God guarding the mother of the promised line a second time. Isaac's protection comes through a pagan king's decree, verse 11, which shows God ruling over those outside the covenant as well.

views.label: One tradition told three ways
views.case: Some modern scholars see Genesis 12, 20 and 26 as variants of a single ancient story. Others answer that the differences are substantial: here no one takes Rebekah, the discovery comes through Abimelech seeing Isaac with her, and the setting and outcome differ. Genesis itself presents the episodes as separate events and draws meaning from their repetition.

debates.bearing: The narrator wants the echo heard. Sons inherit their fathers' sins as well as their blessings, and the promise survives both because God keeps it. That is why the chapter can end with enemies confessing that the LORD is with Isaac.

debates.question: Is Abraham's obedience in verse 5 the ground of the blessing, or its fruit?

views.label: A reward for obedience
views.case: The verse says the blessing comes 'because Abraham listened to My voice,' and it echoes Genesis 22:16-18, 'because you have done this... because you have obeyed My voice.' God does honour obedience, and the text says so.

views.label: Obedience as the fruit of faith
views.case: The promise was given to Abraham long before, Genesis 12:2-3, and he was counted righteous by believing, Genesis 15:6. James says Abraham's 'faith was working with his actions,' James 2:22. On this view verse 5 describes the life of faith that the promise produced, not a wage that earned it.

views.label: Blessing for another's sake
views.case: Verse 24 adds 'for the sake of My servant Abraham.' Isaac receives blessing because of his father's standing with God. This fits the later pattern of blessing 'for the sake of My servant David,' 1 Kings 11:13, and points to Christ, whose obedience brings righteousness to many, Romans 5:19.

debates.bearing: The three views work together. The promise was grace from the start, Abraham's obedience was the fruit of trusting it, and Isaac is blessed because of another. The vocabulary of commandments, statutes and laws teaches Israel that heirs of the promise are marked by listening to God, not that they purchase it.

debates.question: How should we understand the 'Philistines' of Isaac's day?

views.label: A later name for the region
views.case: The Philistines best known from Judges and Samuel were a people who settled the coast later than the patriarchs. On this view the narrator uses the name familiar to his readers for the people of that area, just as he says Beersheba bears its name 'to this day.'

views.label: An earlier group related to the later Philistines
views.case: Others note that Abimelech's people look quite different from the later Philistines: a single king in Gerar rather than five city rulers, and treaty making rather than warfare. They suggest earlier settlers from the same broad population, known by a related name.

debates.bearing: The question is historical and does not change the point of the chapter. Either way, the people of Gerar are outsiders to the covenant who end up acknowledging the LORD's blessing on Isaac.

study.originalLanguages:
God's first word to Isaac uses two verbs for staying. In verse 2 He says, 'Settle in the land,' shakan, the verb of dwelling that later gives the tabernacle its name. In verse 3 He says, 'Stay in this land as a foreigner,' gur, the verb from which ger, the resident alien, comes. Abraham went to Egypt 'to live there for a while,' Genesis 12:10, using the same verb. Isaac is told to be a sojourner in the very land he has been promised, which is why Hebrews 11:9 says the patriarchs lived there 'as a stranger in a foreign country.' The promised 'lands' in verses 3 and 4 are plural, which widens the horizon of the promise.

Verse 5 describes Abraham's obedience in the vocabulary of Sinai. He 'listened to My voice,' shama beqoli, and 'kept My charge,' shamar mishmarti, with 'My commandments, My statutes, and My laws,' mitsvot, chuqqot and torot. Deuteronomy 11:1 uses a very similar list: 'keep His charge, His statutes, His ordinances, and His commandments.' The narrator is describing Abraham's trusting obedience in the words Israel would later use for keeping the law.

In verse 8 Abimelech sees Isaac 'caressing' Rebekah. The word is metsacheq, a form of tsachaq, 'to laugh,' the very root of Isaac's name. It is a pun: Isaac was 'isaacing' his wife. The same form describes Ishmael 'mocking' in Genesis 21:9 and Potiphar's wife accusing Joseph of coming 'to make sport of us,' Genesis 39:14. The verb covers laughter, play and intimacy, and the context shows it here was the familiarity of husband and wife.

Isaac's growth is described with a piling up of words: literally 'the man became great, and went on going and growing great, until he became very great,' verse 13. The root is gadal, the verb of God's promise to Abraham, 'I will make your name great,' Genesis 12:2. The Philistines 'envied' him, qana, a verb that describes Rachel's envy of Leah, Genesis 30:1, and the brothers' jealousy of Joseph, Genesis 37:11. Abimelech then says, 'you are much too powerful for us,' using atsam, the word Pharaoh uses in Exodus 1:9, 'the Israelites have become too numerous and too powerful for us.' The reaction of Gerar anticipates the reaction of Egypt.

The names of the wells are words in their own right, as the BSB footnotes explain. The first well gives 'fresh water,' literally 'living water,' mayim chayyim, verse 19, the phrase behind Jeremiah 2:13, 'the fountain of living water.' Esek comes from the verb 'contend,' and verse 20 says the herdsmen 'contended with him.' Sitnah, 'enmity' or 'hostility,' comes from the same root as satan, 'adversary,' used when the angel stood in Balaam's road 'to oppose him,' Numbers 22:22. Shibah can mean both 'oath' and 'seven,' and Beersheba is the well of the oath.

Abimelech's confession uses an emphatic doubled verb, literally 'seeing, we have seen,' behind the BSB's 'We can plainly see.' And his party leaves 'in peace,' shalom, verses 29 and 31. The chapter's last phrase, 'brought grief,' is literally 'bitterness of spirit,' a heavy note on which to leave Isaac's household.

typology.type: Isaac, blessed for the sake of his father's obedience
typology.fulfillment: Isaac receives the covenant 'because Abraham listened to My voice' and 'for the sake of My servant Abraham,' verses 5 and 24. His blessing rests on another's faithfulness. The gospel carries this pattern to its height: 'through the obedience of the one man the many will be made righteous,' Romans 5:19, and God 'has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing,' Ephesians 1:3. The escalation is that Abraham's obedience was real but mixed with failure, as Genesis 12 and 20 show, while Christ 'became obedient to death,' Philippians 2:8. Believers are blessed not for the sake of a flawed father but for the sake of a perfect Son.

In the Negev a well meant life, and Isaac's servants found 'living water' in the valley, verse 19. Scripture uses that phrase for God Himself, 'the fountain of living water,' Jeremiah 2:13. Jesus sat by a patriarch's well in Samaria and was asked, 'Are You greater than our father Jacob, who gave us this well?' John 4:12. He answered that the water He gives 'will become in him a fount of water springing up to eternal life,' John 4:14. The type falls short because wells could be stopped up and fought over; the living water Christ gives is freely offered and cannot be taken away, Revelation 22:17.

After two contested wells Isaac finds one no one fights over and says, 'At last the LORD has made room for us.' The verb reappears in Isaiah 54:2, 'Enlarge the site of your tent,' a promise to a restored people whose family will grow to include the nations. Jesus speaks of the Father's house, where there are 'many rooms,' and goes 'to prepare a place for you,' John 14:2. The correspondence is God making space for His people when others push them out. The escalation is that Rehoboth was one well in a strip of desert, while Christ prepares room in the Father's own house.

typology.type: Enemies seeking peace because God is with His servant
typology.fulfillment: Abimelech, who had driven Isaac away, comes to him seeking a covenant because 'the LORD has been with you.' Zechariah 8:23 foresees the nations taking hold of a Jew's robe and saying, 'Let us go with you, for we have heard that God is with you.' In Christ this is fulfilled. Peter preached that Jesus 'went around doing good... because God was with Him,' Acts 10:38, and the Gentiles who heard believed. The type falls short, for Abimelech sought a treaty to protect himself, while in Christ the nations are brought near and made one with God's people, Ephesians 2:14.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ first through the promise itself. Verse 4 repeats the heart of the oath to Abraham: 'through your offspring all nations of the earth will be blessed.' Paul says Scripture 'foretold the gospel to Abraham' in those words, Galatians 3:8, and that the offspring in view is ultimately 'One, who is Christ,' Galatians 3:16. Each renewal of the promise to a new patriarch keeps the line open and the hope alive until it comes to rest on Him. 'All the promises of God are "Yes" in Christ,' 2 Corinthians 1:20, including the promise first spoken to a frightened man in a famine at Gerar.

It leads to Christ through the pattern of blessing for another's sake. Isaac did not earn what he received. He was blessed 'for the sake of My servant Abraham,' verse 24, and Abraham's obedience was the channel of it, verse 5. The whole Bible moves toward a better version of this: a servant whose obedience is complete, and a people blessed because they belong to Him. Paul's contrast in Romans 5:19 between the disobedience of one man and the obedience of the one man turns this pattern into the gospel.

It leads to Christ through contrast. Isaac lied to protect himself, afraid that he 'might die on account of her.' He put his wife at risk to save his own life. Christ is the Husband who 'loved the church and gave Himself up for her,' Ephesians 5:25. He did not deny His bride to escape death; He went to death for her. The contrast is sharp enough that the church can read Isaac's failure as a picture of what Christ refused to do.

It leads to Christ through the confession of outsiders. The Philistines say, 'We can plainly see that the LORD has been with you.' Peter says the same thing about Jesus: He went about doing good 'because God was with Him,' Acts 10:38. The difference is that in Jesus God was not merely with a man but had become one, 'Immanuel' which means 'God with us,' Matthew 1:23. Those who once opposed Him came to confess Him, from a Roman centurion at the cross to the nations streaming in through the preaching of the apostles.

Finally, the chapter leads to Christ through the meekness of Isaac at the wells. He did not seize what was his by right; he moved on and trusted God to make room. Jesus said, 'Blessed are the meek, for they will inherit the earth,' Matthew 5:5, echoing Psalm 37:11. The Son who could have summoned legions allowed Himself to be pushed out of the city, and by that road He secured an inheritance wide enough for all nations. A caution belongs here too. Isaac is not a flawless figure of Christ. The links above rest on the promise and on patterns the New Testament itself uses, not on turning every well into a symbol.
study.god:
The chapter shows God as the faithful keeper of His oath. He tells Isaac, 'I will confirm the oath that I swore to your father Abraham.' Hebrews explains why that matters: God 'swore by Himself' to Abraham and guaranteed His promise with an oath, 'to make the unchanging nature of His purpose very clear to the heirs of the promise,' Hebrews 6:13-17. Isaac is the first of those heirs. The change of generation does not change God's commitment.

He is the God who is present. 'I will be with you,' verse 3, and 'Do not be afraid, for I am with you,' verse 24, are the first words God speaks to Isaac at each appearance. His presence comes before His gifts. The land, the offspring and the blessing all depend on the God who goes with His people. The same promise will be spoken to Jacob at Bethel, to Joshua, 'the LORD your God is with you wherever you go,' Joshua 1:9, and to Paul in Corinth, 'Do not be afraid... For I am with you,' Acts 18:9-10.

He is the God who names Himself by His relationships. 'I am the God of your father Abraham,' verse 24. God binds His identity to the people He has called. Jesus draws a profound conclusion from this: if God is still the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, then they are alive to Him, Matthew 22:32. A God who ties His name to mortal men will not let death have the last word over them.

He is generous beyond expectation. The hundredfold harvest comes in a year that began with famine, and the narrator says flatly, 'And the LORD blessed him.' God is not only the God of spiritual promises but the giver of bread and water, flocks and fields. He gives abundantly, and He gives in a way others can see.

He is sovereign over the nations. God warns a Philistine king through His providence, moves him to protect Isaac by decree, and brings him in the end to confess that Isaac is 'blessed by the LORD.' Abimelech's people are outside the covenant, yet God works among them and through them.

He is patient with His servants' failures. Isaac lies, and God does not withdraw the promise. That is not indifference to sin; the narrator lets Abimelech's rebuke stand. But God's faithfulness does not depend on ours. Paul would later write, 'if we are faithless, He remains faithful, for He cannot deny Himself,' 2 Timothy 2:13.

He is the God who makes room. When Isaac is crowded out, God gives him Rehoboth, and when he goes up to Beersheba, God meets him there by night. For worship, the chapter invites trust that the God who keeps His oath across generations keeps it still, gratitude for gifts both material and spiritual, and a willingness to call on His name wherever He makes room for us, as Isaac did when he built an altar, verse 25.

crossReferences.note: The oath God confirms to Isaac in Genesis 26:3-5 is this one, sworn on Mount Moriah after Abraham offered Isaac. The stars of the sky, the blessing of the nations and the phrase 'because you have obeyed My voice' all reappear. Isaac, the son once laid on the altar, now receives the oath in his own name.

Abraham's earlier deception of Abimelech in Gerar is the backdrop for Isaac's. The same excuse, 'They will kill me on account of my wife,' Genesis 20:11, and the same rebuke, 'What have you done to us?', show a son repeating his father's fear. The contrast is that no one takes Rebekah.

Abimelech and Phicol came to Abraham saying, 'God is with you in all that you do,' disputed a well, swore an oath, and the place was named Beersheba. Genesis 26:26-33 retells this with Isaac, so that the covenant and the name are renewed in the second generation.

The psalm remembers 'the covenant He made with Abraham, and the oath He swore to Isaac,' confirmed 'to Jacob as a decree.' Genesis 26 is where the oath is sworn to Isaac, and Israel's worship treated it as a permanent foundation of their life with God.

Pharaoh says the Israelites 'have become too numerous and too powerful for us,' the same complaint Abimelech makes to Isaac in Genesis 26:16. The blessing of God on His people provokes the fear and hostility of the powers around them, and the pattern begun in Gerar reaches its climax in Egypt.

'Enlarge the site of your tent' uses the verb behind Rehoboth. Where Isaac rejoiced that the LORD had made room for his household, Isaiah promises a restored people that God will widen their dwelling for descendants who 'will dispossess the nations.' The room God made at one well becomes room for the world.

At a patriarch's well Jesus offers 'living water,' the phrase the BSB footnote gives for Isaac's well in Genesis 26:19. The Samaritan woman asks if He is greater than Jacob. His answer, water that springs up to eternal life, shows the gift the patriarchs' wells pointed toward.

Men from every nation will grasp a Jew's robe and say, 'Let us go with you, for we have heard that God is with you.' Abimelech's words in Genesis 26:28 are a first instance of the nations seeing that God is with His people and seeking to share in their peace.

Jesus quotes God's self-description as the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob to prove the resurrection. In Genesis 26:24 God first calls Himself 'the God of your father Abraham' to Isaac, linking His name to the patriarchs. Jesus argues that such a God is 'not the God of the dead, but of the living.'

'If it is possible on your part, live at peace with everyone.' Isaac's conduct in Genesis 26 fits this. He moves on rather than fight for each well and receives his former enemies with a feast. Paul's command gives lasting shape to what the patriarch did.

Hebrews says Abraham lived in tents 'as did Isaac and Jacob, who were heirs with him of the same promise.' Genesis 26:3 tells Isaac to 'stay in this land as a foreigner.' Even while blessed with wealth, Isaac remained a sojourner, looking beyond his wells to the city God would prepare.

'When a man's ways please the LORD, He makes even the man's enemies live at peace with him.' The proverb reads like a summary of Genesis 26:26-31, where the men who hated Isaac and drove him away return to make a covenant and leave him in peace.

study.oneStory:
In the story of the whole Bible, Genesis 26 answers a question that every promise raises: will it last beyond the person who first received it? Abraham has died, Genesis 25:8, and the promises of land, offspring and blessing for the nations might have died with him. This chapter says no. God appears to Isaac and swears the same oath, and from now on He is the God of Abraham and of Isaac.

The chapter also shows the world east of Eden still at work. Famine threatens life, fear drives a man to lie, envy fills wells with dirt, and neighbours quarrel over water. The curse on the ground and the fracture between people are still here. Yet in that world God blesses Isaac so that the ground yields a hundredfold, a small foretaste of the curse pushed back.

It sets up what follows. The oath to Isaac will be passed to Jacob at Bethel in Genesis 28, and the three names together become the foundation of Israel's hope, recalled when God hears Israel's groaning in Egypt, Exodus 2:24, and when He promises to remember His covenant after exile, Leviticus 26:42. The chapter's closing note, Esau's Hittite wives, sets the stage for the family crisis of chapter 27 and Jacob's journey to find a wife among his mother's people.

The story finds its centre in Christ. He is the offspring through whom all nations are blessed, the Son whose obedience brings blessing to many, the living water that the wells of the Negev only pictured. In Him God is not merely with His servant; God is with us in person. In Him the outsiders who once opposed God's people are brought near, and the hostility that named the wells Esek and Sitnah is overcome by the One who 'is our peace,' Ephesians 2:14.

The new creation completes the picture. Isaac lived as a foreigner in the land he was promised, and Hebrews says the patriarchs 'were longing for a better country, a heavenly one,' Hebrews 11:16. There, no one will stop up the wells. The Lamb 'will lead them to springs of living water,' Revelation 7:17, and to the thirsty God will give 'freely from the spring of the water of life,' Revelation 21:6. The meek will inherit the earth, and the nations will walk in the light of the city of God, Revelation 21:24, confessing forever that the LORD has been with His people.

quiz.q: What did the LORD promise Isaac during the famine?

options.text: To be with him, bless him, and confirm the oath He had sworn to Abraham.
options.note: Verses 3 to 4 renew the Abrahamic promises directly to Isaac.

options.text: That the famine would end within a single year.
options.note: God promises His presence and blessing; He does not simply date the famine's end.

options.text: That Isaac should go down to Egypt for safety.
options.note: God tells him the opposite, not to go down to Egypt but to stay in the land.

options.text: That the land would pass to the Philistines.
options.note: God promises the land to Isaac and his offspring, not to the Philistines.

quiz.q: How did Isaac repeat one of his father Abraham's failures?

options.text: He lied that Rebekah was his sister out of fear for his life.
options.note: Verse 7 echoes Abraham's sister-wife deception, driven by fear.

options.text: He offered his son as a sacrifice.
options.note: That was Abraham's test in chapter 22; Isaac's echoed failure here is the sister-wife lie.

options.text: He drove Hagar and Ishmael away.
options.note: That belonged to Abraham's household, not Isaac's; his repeated failure is the lie about his wife.

options.text: He refused to leave Egypt.
options.note: Isaac never goes to Egypt; God tells him to stay in the land.

quiz.q: Why did Isaac name a well Rehoboth?

options.text: Because the LORD had at last made room for him after repeated quarrels over water.
options.note: Rehoboth means broad places; Isaac praises God for room to be fruitful.

options.text: Because it was the first well his servants ever dug.
options.note: It was not the first; it followed the disputed wells Esek and Sitnah.

options.text: Because the Philistines had given it to him as a gift.
options.note: The Philistines contended over the earlier wells; Rehoboth was one they did not quarrel over, not a gift.

options.text: Because it marked the place of a battle he had won.
options.note: It marks peace and room, not a battle.

quiz.q: Why did Abimelech come to make a covenant with Isaac?

options.text: Because he could plainly see that the LORD was with Isaac.
options.note: Verse 28 gives their stated reason, echoing the earlier treaty with Abraham.

options.text: Because Isaac had defeated him in war.
options.note: There is no war; Abimelech seeks peace because God is evidently with Isaac.

options.text: Because Isaac demanded tribute from Gerar.
options.note: Isaac makes no such demand; Abimelech comes seeking a peace oath.

options.text: Because he wanted to take Rebekah as his wife.
options.note: Abimelech had earlier protected Rebekah; the covenant is about peace, not marriage.

quiz.q: What does this chapter show about God's covenant promise?

options.text: It passes faithfully to Isaac by God's grace, holding firm despite Isaac's fear and failures.
options.note: The promise rests on God's faithfulness, not on Isaac's flawless obedience.

options.text: It depended on Isaac never sinning.
options.note: Isaac does sin, yet the promise stands; it rests on grace, not sinlessness.

options.text: It was transferred away from Isaac to Abimelech.
options.note: The promise remains with Isaac; Abimelech only seeks peace with him.

options.text: It ended because of the famine and the strife.
options.note: The covenant is renewed and confirmed through the famine and strife, not ended.

questions: God told Isaac not to fear because He was with him. Where do you most need to hear that same word of God's presence in your life right now?
Isaac fell into the very fear driven lie his father had told. What patterns from those before you do you find yourself repeating, and how might God break the cycle?
After strife over wells, Isaac praised God for making room at Rehoboth. Where are you longing for God to make room and give peace after a season of conflict?
Isaac's blessing was so evident that even his enemies sought peace with him. What would it look like for others to see clearly that God is with you?
God kept His promise to Isaac despite Isaac's weakness. How does it free you to know that God's faithfulness to you does not rest on your perfect performance?

translationNotes.note: The wells are named for what happened at them: Esek means contention, Sitnah means hostility, and Rehoboth means broad places or room, tracing Isaac's path from strife to peace.
Shibah plays on the Hebrew words for oath and for seven, tying the well's name to the sworn covenant and to the earlier naming of Beersheba in Abraham's day.
